title: Morphogen Gradients and Developmental Robustness
markdown: ## What this covers This is the closing lecture of the course. It states the four lessons the course meant to teach, then turns to the last new topic: developmental systems biology, using the patterning of the early *Drosophila* (fruit fly) embryo as the running example. Two case studies are worked: how a smoothly graded maternal signal (Bicoid) is converted into a sharp on/off decision by a target gene (Hunchback), and how a reaction–diffusion network of three interacting proteins (Sog, Scw, Tld) patterns the embryo's dorsal–ventral axis in a way that turns out to be robust to gene dosage. It assumes the reaction–diffusion and stability-analysis machinery built up earlier in the course — writing coupled partial differential equations for interacting, diffusing species and asking what shape their steady state takes — and the notion of robustness introduced when the course covered bacterial chemotaxis. ## Where this sits in the course The lecturer opened by placing this lecture against the whole course, which the slides lay out in three parts: - **I. Systems microbiology** (13 lectures) — *"the cell as a well-stirred biochemical reactor"*: introduction; chemical kinetics, equilibrium binding, cooperativity; lambda phage; stability analysis; genetic switches; *E. coli* chemotaxis; genetic oscillators; stochastic chemical kinetics. - **II. Systems cell biology** (9 lectures) — *"the cell as a compartmentalized system with concentration gradients"*: diffusion and Fick's equations with boundary and initial conditions; local-excitation/global-inhibition theory; models of eukaryotic gradient sensing; center-finding algorithms; cytoskeleton dynamics. - **III. Systems developmental biology** (2 lectures) — *"the cell in a social context communicating with neighboring cells"*: quorum sensing, and — this lecture — *Drosophila* development. and then restated the course's four take-home messages directly: 1. **Translate the biology into a quantitative model.** Given the biology, set up the coupled differential equations that capture the essence of the phenomenon. This step is not trivial: the lecturer noted that four different papers proposed four different models for the *same* biological phenomenon — which simplifying assumptions to make is exactly what is at stake. 2. **Analyse the resulting system of differential equations** — stability analysis, in both space and time. 3. **Interpret the mathematical analysis biologically.** A non-zero imaginary part of an eigenvalue, for instance, is a mathematical fact; the question the course kept asking is what it *means* for the underlying biology. 4. **Develop a taste for where this kind of approach pays off**, for biological problems not yet encountered. The rest of the lecture works a second illustration of point 1: two different groups modeled patterning in the same embryo and, exactly as the take-home message warns, made different choices about what to include. ## Building an embryo from one cell: why *Drosophila* The new material opens with the general problem of developmental biology: *building an organism starting from a single cell*. The fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster* is the running example — the lecturer recommended Peter Lawrence's book *The Making of the Fly* as further reading, and pointed to a movie of the process at flymove.uni-muenster.de. The particular advantage of *Drosophila* for this course is that the embryo is visibly segmented into stripes, and each stripe maps onto an identifiable body part of the adult fly — patterning can be watched happening directly, rather than inferred after the fact. The idea that positional information along an embryo is set by chemical signals goes back to Klaus Sander's pioneering experiments on leafhoppers in 1958: ligating (tying off) or transplanting pieces of an insect embryo showed that something was being made and destroyed at the two poles, and that this something carried spatial information. The modern term for such a signal is **morphogen**. ## Bicoid: a maternal morphogen The first morphogen identified in *Drosophila* is **Bicoid**, and it is a genuinely *maternal* signal: the mother deposits bicoid mRNA at the anterior pole of the egg before the embryo's own genome is doing anything, and it is translated there to set up a concentration gradient that is highest at the anterior and decays toward the posterior. Two classical observations established this: - **Transplantation.** Moving bicoid (or the anterior cytoplasm containing it) to a new location is enough to rescue anterior structures there — bicoid is not merely correlated with the anterior fate, it is sufficient to create it. - **Dosage.** Increasing the number of copies of the bicoid gene in the mother shifts the position of the head fold in the offspring toward the posterior: more gene copies means more protein, a gradient that stays above threshold for longer, so the boundary it sets moves. ## Reading the gradient: Hunchback and an open puzzle Bicoid is a maternal signal; it says nothing by itself about what the embryo's *own* genome should do next. That interpretation is zygotic — carried out by genes expressed by the embryo itself. The gene **Hunchback** is the one that reads the Bicoid gradient, and it does something the gradient itself does not: it turns a smooth, graded input into a sharp, step-like boundary of expression positioned close to the middle of the embryo. Houchmandzadeh et al. (*Nature* 415, 798, 2002) is cited as the paper that made the Bicoid–Hunchback relationship quantitative. The puzzle the lecture leaves open is put on the slide almost verbatim: **how can a steep step in Hunchback, positioned exactly in the middle of the embryo, be produced from a Bicoid gradient that is inherently noisy?** The slide's answer is blunt — *nobody knows*. It is presented as a live open question, not something the lecture goes on to resolve. ## A second example: robustness of dorsal–ventral patterning The second case study returns to a theme the course had already met once, in bacterial chemotaxis: **robustness** — a patterning outcome that stays the same even though the underlying rates and concentrations vary. Eldar et al. (*Nature* 419, 304, 2002) asked whether the same kind of robustness shows up in *Drosophila* patterning, this time along the embryo's dorsal–ventral axis. Three molecules carry the model: - **Scw**, a BMP (bone morphogenetic protein) — the diffusible ligand that specifies dorsal–ventral identity. - **Sog**, an inhibitor of BMP signaling — it binds Scw and blocks it from acting. - **Tld**, a protease that cleaves Sog. ## The reaction–diffusion model Writing $[Sog]$, $[Scw]$ and $[Sog\text{-}Scw]$ for the concentrations of free Sog, free Scw, and the bound complex, the model is three coupled reaction–diffusion equations along the embryo axis $x$: $$ \frac{\partial [Sog]}{\partial t} = D_S \frac{\partial^2 [Sog]}{\partial x^2} - k_b [Sog][Scw] + k_{-b}[Sog\text{-}Scw] - \alpha [Tld][Sog] $$ $$ \frac{\partial [Scw]}{\partial t} = D_{BMP} \frac{\partial^2 [Scw]}{\partial x^2} - k_b [Sog][Scw] + k_{-b}[Sog\text{-}Scw] + \lambda [Tld][Sog\text{-}Scw] $$ $$ \frac{\partial [Sog\text{-}Scw]}{\partial t} = D_C \frac{\partial^2 [Sog\text{-}Scw]}{\partial x^2} + k_b [Sog][Scw] - k_{-b}[Sog\text{-}Scw] - \lambda [Tld][Sog\text{-}Scw] $$ Each term has a direct reading: - $D_S$, $D_{BMP}$, $D_C$: each species diffuses along the embryo, with its own coefficient. - $k_b[Sog][Scw]$: Sog and Scw bind (an ordinary bimolecular reaction), removing free Sog and Scw and creating complex. - $k_{-b}[Sog\text{-}Scw]$: the complex can also fall back apart, regenerating free Sog and Scw. - $\alpha[Tld][Sog]$: Tld can degrade *free* Sog directly. - $\lambda[Tld][Sog\text{-}Scw]$: Tld can also cleave the Sog sitting inside the complex — this removes the complex and, in the same step, releases the Scw it was holding as active, free ligand. This is the step that couples "inhibitor destroyed" to "ligand liberated." ## The idealised limit, and why the question is left open The slides pose the robustness question directly — *what makes this pattern insensitive to changes in how much ligand or inhibitor is made?* — and start toward an answer by stripping the model down to an idealised limit: set $D_{BMP}=0$ (free Scw itself does not diffuse; only the complex carries it across the embryo), $\alpha=0$ (Tld does not touch free Sog, only the Sog inside a complex), and $k_{-b}=0$ (the complex does not spontaneously fall apart — the only way out of it is via Tld). The three equations reduce, at steady state, to: $$ 0 = D_S \frac{\partial^2 [Sog]}{\partial x^2} - k_b [Sog][Scw] $$ $$ 0 = -k_b [Sog][Scw] + \lambda [Tld][Sog\text{-}Scw] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\frac{1}{[Scw]} = \frac{k_b}{D_S} $$ $$ 0 = D_C \frac{\partial^2 [Sog\text{-}Scw]}{\partial x^2} + k_b [Sog][Scw] - \lambda [Tld][Sog\text{-}Scw] $$ The surviving slides state the reduced equations and the resulting equation for $1/[Scw]$ but do not show the algebra connecting them, and do not go on to say why *this* reduced system is robust to dosage. That argument — the point the case study was building toward — is not in the material available for this chapter. ## Sources - Course structure, the three-part outline (systems microbiology / systems cell biology / systems developmental biology) and the four take-home messages: slide deck `01-i-systems-microbiology-13-lectures.md` (MIT OCW 8.591J, Fall 2004, lecture notes "25-notes", part I). - *Drosophila* as a model system, Klaus Sander's 1958 leafhopper experiments, Bicoid as a maternal morphogen (transplantation and dosage evidence), Hunchback reading the Bicoid gradient, and the open puzzle of the sharp Hunchback boundary: slide deck `02-developmental-systems-biology.md`, citing Houchmandzadeh et al., *Nature* 415, 798 (2002). - The Sog–Scw–Tld robustness model, its reaction–diffusion equations, and the idealised limit: the same slide deck, citing Eldar et al., *Nature* 419, 304 (2002). - Referred to but not contained in the supplied material: Peter Lawrence's book *The Making of the Fly*; the developmental movie at flymove.uni-muenster.de; the earlier lecture on chemotaxis robustness (L9–10) that this lecture explicitly recalls; and the algebra connecting the reduced Sog/Scw equations to $\partial^2(1/[Scw])/\partial x^2 = k_b/D_S$, along with the argument for why the idealised system is robust to gene dosage — neither appears on the surviving slides. - No transcript, notes or exercises were supplied for this lecture.
